title: Not annihilation (section 27)
hook: don't think the bodhisattva destroys things; emptiness is not nothing

segments.voice: Yesterday, form and sound: the Tathagata isn't found by the eye's catch or the ear's catch, but seen from the Dharma. Your line: not by form or sound.

Somewhere tonight a college sophomore reads one chapter of Buddhist philosophy, shuts the book, and tells the roommate: nothing is real. So the dishes don't matter. The roommate, who has seen the sink, has thoughts. It's an old wrong turn, and the Diamond Sutra has been walking right past it for weeks: no self, no marks, no merit held, no teaching owned. Keep cutting like that and someone will call the whole thing a wrecking ball. In section twenty-seven, the Buddha blocks that road by name.
screen: `NOTHING IS REAL, SO NO DISHES.` → `ALL THAT CUTTING.` → `A ROAD BLOCKED BY NAME.`

segments.voice: The sutra has cut almost everything a person could hold: a self, the bodily marks, merit, the teaching itself, even the raft. A listener could decide the bodhisattva's job is to tear things down. So, in paraphrase, the Buddha tells Subhuti: don't think the highest awakening was reached through the marks. And let no one tell you that those on the bodhisattva path teach the destruction or annihilation of anything. Not of a single thing. The cutting was never demolition. This isn't a new idea dropped in at the end. In an early discourse, the Buddha tells a monk named Kaccana that everything exists is one extreme, and nothing exists is the other. The Tathagata teaches by the middle, without going to either. It's the middle way you've met many times on this path, and section twenty-seven stands on the same ground. When the sutra says a thing has no fixed self, it hasn't said the thing is gone. Empty, in this teaching, means empty of a fixed, separate core, not empty of being here. A cup that is only so called still holds the tea. The bodhisattva who frees no beings is still at work helping them. So the roommate is right, and so, in a way, is the sutra. Nothing is fixed. The dishes are still real. And somebody still has to wash them.
screen: `ALL THAT CUTTING.` · `NO THING DESTROYED.` · `THE MIDDLE, NOT THE EXTREMES.` · `EMPTY OF A CORE, STILL HERE.` · then, large: `NOT NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Let your attention land on one ordinary thing near you: the chair holding you up, the floor, a plant on the sill. Notice it has no fixed core you could pull out and keep; it's made of other things, and it's changing. Then notice, just as clearly, that it's here, warm or worn or doing its job, and let both be true at once, maybe with a quiet thank you.
Not annihilation. Section twenty-seven: those on the bodhisattva path don't teach the destruction of anything. Empty of a fixed core is not the same as nothing. Today's word.
Your line: not nothing. Empty of a core, and still right here. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers present emptiness as a middle way between the views that everything exists and that nothing exists, and section 27 of the Diamond Sutra is read as a guard against hearing emptiness as nothingness.

pairs: the monk told about the middle

fork.setup: after all the sutra's cutting, a friend says: so the bodhisattva path destroys everything. what does section 27 say?
options: no: they don't teach the annihilation of anything
only the bad things get destroyed
fork.reveal: the Buddha says let no one tell you that those on the bodhisattva path teach the destruction or annihilation of any thing.

original.note: Sanskrit and Pali: cutting off, annihilation; the extreme section 27 says the bodhisattva path does not teach.

trapdoor: what you thought: emptiness means nothing is really there.
what it means: things lack a fixed core; they aren't destroyed or erased.
what a scholar hears: section 27 guards against the annihilation view, the extreme the Buddha sets beside 'everything exists' in the Kaccana discourse.

chat.says: Buddhism says everything is empty. Doesn't that mean nothing really matters?
options: No. Empty means no fixed core, not gone; the sutra says the bodhisattva path destroys nothing.
Yes. Once you see things are empty, caring about them is just more clinging.
Only in meditation; off the cushion, things go back to being solid and fixed.
chat.meaning: Section twenty-seven blocks annihilation by name; like the middle way taught to Kaccana, empty means no fixed core, not nothing.

Tathagata.meaning: the awakened one; a title the Buddha uses for himself

Subhuti.meaning: the elder who questions the Buddha in the Diamond Sutra

bodhisattva.meaning: one who vows to awaken for the sake of all beings

Kaccana.meaning: a monk the Buddha taught the middle between two extremes

notes: Section 27 paraphrased, not quoted from Max Müller (wording unverified): check both halves (awakening not through the marks; no destruction or annihilation of any dharma taught by those on the bodhisattva path).
Kaccanagotta Sutta (SN 12.15) paraphrased: 'everything exists' and 'nothing exists' as two extremes, the Tathagata teaching by the middle. Confirm.
Original-language word: uccheda as the Sanskrit term for annihilation in section 27 (alongside vinasa); confirm the term in the Sanskrit text and the pronunciation.
'Empty of a fixed, separate core' is a teaching gloss on emptiness, not a quotation; confirm the fair description.
